blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Smaller language models (SLMs) make it feasible to deploy clinical natural language processing where large proprietary models are too costly, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning allows them to be specialised on commodity hardware. One obstacle persists after training: on medical tasks these models answer at far greater length than the clinical question requires. In clinical decision support and point-of-care use, where time is short, such verbosity is hard to act on even when the underlying reasoning is sound. Existing length-control methods depend on preference optimisation, reward models, or proprietary teachers that undercut the accessibility making SLMs attractive. We introduce Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation (PECA), which adds a single differentiable conciseness term to the QLoRA supervised fine-tuning objective. Because the token count is discrete and non-differentiable, PECA instead raises the end-of-sequence probability once generation exceeds a token budget, a smooth signal optimised during ordinary training, with no preference data, no auxiliary model, and a single commodity GPU. On a 1.7-billion-parameter model fine-tuned on the medical-o1-reasoning-SFT corpus, PECA reduces mean response length by 72.8% while improving multiple-choice diagnostic accuracy from 40.8% to 44.0%. A sweep over the conciseness strength traces an interpretable accuracy-to-length frontier for balancing brevity and diagnostic completeness.

blocks.en: Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Healthcare is absorbing language technology at a remarkable pace.
Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) already assist with clinical
question answering, medical documentation, patient triage, and decision support,
and on a number of diagnostic benchmarks their scores now rival, or even surpass,
those of trained clinicians. This ability is largely inherited from large-scale
pretraining, which yields representations general enough to carry over from
ordinary text into the more specialised vocabulary of medicine [1, 2]. In the
clinic this strength cuts both ways. The models that score best are usually the
ones a hospital can least easily run, audit, or host on its own servers, and the
reason is not only their price. Patient data cannot leave the building, and the
largest systems are precisely the ones that are hardest to keep inside it.

blocks.en:
Hardware is the first wall. An LLM with tens of billions of parameters may need
hundreds of gigabytes of memory and dedicated accelerators to serve, and that
bill by itself is enough to place it out of reach for most hospitals, clinics,
and the smaller research groups around them [3]. It is this practical ceiling,
more than any lack of capability, that has drawn attention toward smaller
language models (SLMs) of roughly one to thirteen billion parameters. Such models
retain a good deal of what makes their larger counterparts useful, yet they
remain light enough to run on commodity hardware and, at least in principle, on
machines that never leave the provider’s own premises [12]. For clinicians,
low-resource hospitals, and medical research groups working under tight budgets
and strict data-governance constraints, SLMs are a realistic way to deploy
advanced clinical language technology, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)
has been central to making that possible.

blocks.en:
Adapting an SLM to a specialised domain exposes a problem that accuracy
benchmarks tend to hide. PEFT solves the cost of training; what it leaves
untouched is a habit that surfaces afterwards, namely that domain-adapted SLMs
answer at much greater length than the question warrants. The issue is sharpest
wherever information has to be delivered fast and without ambiguity. Clinical NLP
has made this very clear. Compact models fine-tuned on medical reasoning have
matched or beaten specialist physicians on diagnostic benchmarks [18], yet those
same clinicians note that the verbosity of the explanations makes them
impractical at the bedside, where a decision cannot wait for a long exposition.
Being correct is necessary, but an answer that takes longer than the time
available has failed regardless of how accurate it is.

This verbosity is a gap the PEFT literature has mostly passed over. LoRA [2] and
its quantised form QLoRA [12] save a great deal by confining weight updates to
low-rank matrices, but neither shapes how long the outputs run. Length follows
from the training distribution alone, never from an explicit objective. The
methods that do target length usually sit at the preference-optimisation stage
[14, 32, 33], which needs paired preferences or a learned reward model, or they
distil from a stronger proprietary teacher [11], which needs API access. Either
way the dependencies cut against the low-resource, open case for using SLMs at
all.

blocks.en:
We close this gap with Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation (PECA). It
folds conciseness straight into the supervised fine-tuning objective through one
auxiliary term, with no preference data, no auxiliary model, and nothing external
at inference. The design hinges on how length is penalised. A penalty written
over the number of generated tokens cannot be optimised by gradient descent,
since token count is discrete and its gradient with respect to the parameters is
zero almost everywhere. So PECA acts on the model’s probability of stopping
instead: once generation passes a token budget, the objective raises the
probability assigned to the end-of-sequence token, a continuous signal that
shapes stopping behaviour during normal training. The procedure adds almost
nothing to the cost of QLoRA fine-tuning and reproduces on a single commodity
GPU.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows. • We identify post-training verbosity as a practical limitation of
PEFT-adapted medical SLMs and treat it as a problem separate from task
accuracy. • We propose PECA, a preference-free and fully differentiable
conciseness objective for QLoRA supervised fine-tuning. We show why a naive
penalty on the discrete token count cannot work, and we give a correct
end-of-sequence surrogate that is easy to implement and runs on consumer
GPUs. • We provide a systematic evaluation across four values of the
conciseness strength λ \lambda , revealing a clear Pareto frontier between
response length and diagnostic accuracy, and identifying λ = 0.25 \lambda=0.25 as
the setting that achieves 72.8% length reduction with improved MedMCQA
accuracy.

blocks.en: Related Work
blocks.zh: 相关工作

blocks.en:
Full fine-tuning is expensive, and a large body of work has grown up around
avoiding it. The account below follows that work from the early selective-update
proposals through to recent hybrid designs, then turns to a question it has
largely neglected: how long the model’s outputs actually are.

避开它。 以下说明沿用了早期选择性更新后的工作
然后转而提出一个问题
大部分被忽略:模型的输出实际有多长.

blocks.en: Foundations of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
blocks.zh: 参数有效图解基础

blocks.en:
Early work on parameter efficiency focused on restricting which weights are
updated during fine-tuning. Ben-Zaken et al. [3] introduced BitFit, which
modifies only the bias terms, touching roughly 0.1% of all parameters. Effective
on classification, it reached only 61% of full fine-tuning performance on
machine translation, revealing the limits of very sparse updates for generative
tasks.

blocks.en:
Houlsby et al. [2, 13] addressed this by inserting small trainable modules between
the frozen transformer layers. Touching just 3 to 4% of the parameters, these
adapters still recover 85 to 90% of full fine-tuning performance on multitask
benchmarks. The catch is at inference. Every adapter sits in the forward path and
has to be run in turn, which drives latency up by 23 to 40%, far too much when an
answer is needed on the spot.

blocks.en:
Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), from Hu et al. [2], is what eventually stuck. Rather
than update a weight matrix directly, LoRA learns two small matrices whose product
approximates the change. That leaves only 0.1 to 0.6% of the parameters
trainable, and yet on GPT-2, GPT-3, RoBERTa, and DeBERTa the method matches full
fine-tuning and occasionally edges past it. Its real advantage is that the two
matrices merge back into the base weights once training ends, so inference pays no
extra cost at all [2, 17]. The idea has since been pulled in several directions.
RaLo [25] varies the adapter rank as training proceeds; HydraLoRA [28] makes the
two sides asymmetric to squeeze out more efficiency; and the recipe has escaped
NLP entirely, driving language-specific translation in low-resource settings [5]
and even turning up in image-restoration work [27].

blocks.en: Advanced Integration and Hybrid Approaches
blocks.zh: 高级一体化和混合办法

blocks.en:
Dettmers et al. [12] built QLoRA by extending LoRA with 4-bit quantisation,
cutting memory use by more than 94% and so allowing 65-billion-parameter models
to be fine-tuned on a single 48 GB GPU with no loss of performance [12]. PEFT
greatly increases Phi-1.5 when answering scientific questions: BLEU scores
increase from 0.0027 to 0.132, ROUGE-L from 0.152 to 0.235, and BERT F1 from
0.5266 to 0.6002. In medical and legal QA, He et al.’s hybrids [3] that combine
dynamic rank allocation and chain-of-thought retrieval-augmented generation
improve BLEU scores by up to 37.5% over standard LoRA. Quantisation has pushed
this further still, letting biomedical summarisation run on low-power devices
where memory would otherwise be a hard constraint [26].

arrive without a quality penalty [8, 12]. Nor does everything hinge on

blocks.en: Length Control and Conciseness in Language Generation
blocks.zh: 语言生成的长度控制和简明性

blocks.en:
A quite separate literature concerns itself with how long a model’s output is
rather than whether it is correct. The bulk of this work operates at the
preference-optimisation stage. Direct Preference Optimization and its relatives
have a well-documented tendency to reward longer answers, and several methods try
to correct for it: Park et al. [33] pull length apart from quality and bolt a
length regulariser onto the DPO objective, SimPO [32] instead adopts a
length-normalised, reference-free reward, and Length-Controlled Margin-based
Preference Optimization (LMPO) [19] adds a length-aware margin for the same
purpose. Reinforcement learning offers a parallel and much newer route to the
problem. SmartThinker [37] swaps the fixed length rewards used by earlier
GRPO-style methods for a calibration that adapts to problem difficulty, precisely
so as to avoid the over-compression a rigid penalty tends to cause, something we
too run into once the conciseness strength is pushed high. All of these ideas
work, but each one leans on preference pairs, a reward model, a reference policy,
or RL rollouts, and every one of those requirements sits awkwardly with the
low-resource, preference-free scenario we are after. Closest to our objective,
Belligoli et al. [31] control summary length by giving more weight to the
end-of-sequence (EOS) token inside the cross-entropy loss, a fully differentiable
mechanism that works with supervised data alone. The present work extends this
principle into the QLoRA parameter-efficient fine-tuning setting, applying a
budget-gated EOS term to clinical chain-of-thought models where preference data
and external teachers are unavailable.

blocks.en: Domain-Specific Applications

blocks.en:
Clinical and biomedical NLP has adopted PEFT extensively. Specialised adaptations
such as Med-PaLM and BioBERT draw on QLoRA, prefix tuning, and reinforcement
learning from human feedback to improve diagnostic, educational, and documentation
tasks [6]. Liu et al. [29] apply parameter-efficient instruction tuning to
biomedical named entity recognition, obtaining strong extraction accuracy at low
computational overhead. Domain resources such as consumer medical question
answering datasets have further supported this line of work [16]. Li et al. [24] show that small-parameter LLMs can be
fine-tuned effectively for bilingual biomedical tasks across languages, and more
recent work has carried PEFT into the multimodal clinical setting, as in PeFoMed
[36] for medical visual question answering and radiology report generation, and
other recent systems fine-tune general language models directly for grounded
clinical diagnosis [38]. The
medical chain-of-thought corpus used in the present study originates from the

blocks.en: Limitations in Existing PEFT Approaches
blocks.zh: 现有PEFT方法的局限性

blocks.en:
Despite these advances, PEFT methods remain susceptible to domain-specific
inconsistencies [1, 4] and to catastrophic forgetting in multi-task settings,
where shared adapters can degrade performance by as much as 14% [3, 4]. A more
fundamental omission, however, concerns output quality rather than accuracy.
Verbosity in particular has received little systematic attention: a fine-tuned
SLM may reason competently and still generate responses too long to be acted on
under time pressure [18]. PEFT has also been studied as an enabler of foundation
models in federated learning [30], which underscores its breadth across
deployment settings. The practical value of PEFT in high-stakes domains is
constrained as much by this post-training communication failure as by any
shortfall in raw accuracy.

blocks.en: Positioning of This Study Within Prior Work
blocks.zh: 这项研究在以前工作中的位置

blocks.en:
Every one of these methods has something to recommend it. LoRA balances quality
against cost, QLoRA earns its place when resources are scarce, and adapters make
multitasking straightforward. None, though, ties parameter-efficient adaptation
to post-training conciseness in one procedure, and that gap is widest for the
sub-2B SLMs we care about. Length-control work stops at the preference-optimisation
stage and assumes preference data or a reward model is on hand; PEFT work chases
accuracy and looks no further. Our contribution bridges the two, attaching a
differentiable EOS-budget conciseness term to QLoRA fine-tuning and charting a
length-versus-accuracy Pareto frontier that a clinical deployment can tune to
taste.

Read down the final column of Table 3 , PECA is the only method
that is at once preference-free, teacher-free, differentiable within supervised
fine-tuning, free of any inference-time overhead, and parameter-efficient. The
closest prior method conceptually is the end-of-sequence weighting of Belligoli
et al. [31], which shares the differentiable, supervised, preference-free
character of our term; the difference is that it was developed for full
fine-tuning of a summarisation model, whereas PECA gates the signal by a token
budget and situates it inside QLoRA so that it runs on commodity hardware for
clinical chain-of-thought models. Relative to the reinforcement-learning line,
SmartThinker [37] reports up to 52.5% length reduction with accuracy gains on
mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, and our method achieves a larger relative
reduction (72.8%) with a diagnostic-accuracy gain on a clinical benchmark; the
two figures are not directly comparable because the model families and tasks
differ, but the comparison does show that a simple supervised term can reach the
compression regime that RL methods target without their rollout and
reward-modelling machinery. Against the preference-optimisation methods

blocks.en: Discussion
blocks.zh: 讨论情况

blocks.en:
We set out to deal with a practical obstacle in deploying specialised small
language models: after domain adaptation they tend to answer at a length that
does not suit practitioners who have to move quickly. Parameter-Efficient
Conciseness Adaptation (PECA) is our answer, a preference-free method built around
a differentiable, budget-gated signal on the end-of-sequence probability.
Penalising the raw token count will not work, since a discrete count carries no
gradient; PECA gets around this by reinforcing the stopping probability once
generation passes a budget, an objective that lives inside ordinary supervised
fine-tuning and costs almost nothing to add.

blocks.en:
Working with a 1.7-billion-parameter model and 8,000 medical chain-of-thought
examples, we found a length-versus-accuracy trade-off orderly enough that a
practitioner can navigate it deliberately instead of by guesswork. Our recommended
setting, λ = 0.25 \lambda=0.25 , trims mean length by 72.8% and, to our own surprise,
lifts MedMCQA accuracy by 3.2 points over vanilla QLoRA fine-tuning. Larger λ \lambda keeps trimming the output, but now accuracy is the price, and at the
extreme the model falls apart. The cost side is worth stating plainly: no run took
more than three hours on one commodity GPU under 6 GB, and none of them called for
preference data, a second model, or a paid endpoint.

What we take to be the most telling implication is that a domain-adapted SLM’s
verbosity is mostly a residue of its training distribution, not some necessary
companion of good reasoning. A gentle nudge toward stopping is enough to break the
habit, and doing so nudges multiple-choice accuracy upward rather than down, most
likely because the text being cut is hedging and repetition, words that pad a
response without adding anything a clinician could act on. The contribution of
PECA, in operational terms, is to expose a single interpretable parameter through
which a deployment can be placed at its preferred location on the brevity-accuracy
frontier.

blocks.en: Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation (PECA)
blocks.zh: 参数-有效简明性适应(PECA)

blocks.en:
We present Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation (PECA), a framework that
addresses excessive response verbosity in domain-specific small language models,
a behaviour that impedes clinical use even when the underlying diagnostic
reasoning is sound [15, 18]. In contrast to approaches that rely on
resource-intensive preference optimisation, such as Direct Preference
Optimization [14, 33], SimPO [32], and LMPO [19], or on distillation from
proprietary large language models [11], PECA achieves clinically appropriate
brevity through a single, fully differentiable term added to standard supervised
fine-tuning (SFT) under quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) [2, 12].

blocks.en: Implementation and Reproducibility
blocks.zh: 执行和可复制

blocks.en:
All experiments were run on NVIDIA A10G and L4 GPUs using PyTorch, Hugging Face
Transformers, PEFT, and BitsAndBytes. Peak GPU memory across all conditions was
4.4 to 5.3 GB, well within a 16 GB budget, confirming that PECA is accessible
on widely available hardware. Each condition completed in approximately 153 to
163 minutes. The full source code, processed dataset splits,
training logs, and trained QLoRA adapters will be made publicly available upon
publication at https://github.com/tanzeelabbas/PECA-Medical and on Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/tanzeelabbas114 .
